A1.justification: Both PDFs contain the same HAMLET research work, with 32 pages and Appendices A–L. Complete text and rendered-page comparisons support reliable assessment; differences are confined to pages 1, 30 and 32.

before.justification: v4 reports original bilingual drama evaluations, critic–human correlations, PAD experiments and component ablations in Section 5, plus empirical analyses in Appendices G–I.

after.justification: v5 retains these original experimental results, including Tables 1–3, the component ablations and the appendix agreement, latency and task-completion measurements.

M1.justification: Section 3, Algorithms 1–2 and the actual agent prompts are unchanged. Omitting 'emotional states' from the abstract and correcting a prompt-box heading do not establish changes to the method.

E1.justification: Both retain the same English and Chinese drama coverage: 50 literary excerpts and 50 custom topics, alongside the same PAD and HAMLETJudge training datasets and test scenarios.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged throughout the leaderboard, reliability experiments and ablations. For example, Table 2 retains GPT-4.1, Claude-4-Sonnet and Gemini-2.5-Pro as HAMLETJudge comparators.

E3.justification: The evaluation dimensions, 75-item evaluation sets per language, holdout splits, training budgets and ablation controls remain identical. No experimental setting or testing procedure is revised.

E4.justification: The PAD/framework and reviewer ablations in Figures 6–7, Advancer ablation in Appendix I, six interaction cases in Appendix C and supplementary latency analyses are retained unchanged.

E5.justification: The five-expert annotation setup and Krippendorff’s Alpha/Fleiss’ Kappa reporting in Appendix G.3 are unchanged. No repeated-run, seed, confidence-interval or other uncertainty-reporting information is added or removed.

E6.justification: All reported numerical results, plots and qualitative examples are unchanged. Examples include HAMLETJudge’s average correlation of 0.791 in Table 2, PAD’s final score of 0.756 in Table 3 and the 100.0% versus 68.1% completion rates in Table 13.

T1.justification: The PAD formalization and the logarithmic latency-penalty definition in Appendix G.4, Equation 1, are identical. No mathematical assumptions, derivations, theorems or proofs are added or revised.

C1.justification: The central claims about autonomous embodied drama, PAD and HAMLETJudge remain intact. The abstract shortens its input summary by omitting 'emotional states,' without changing the substantive contributions retained in the introduction and conclusion.

C2.justification: Interpretations of reasoning efficiency, quality–latency tradeoffs, reviewer effects and Advancer failure modes remain unchanged, as do the latency-measurement limitations discussed in Appendix G.4.

D1.justification: Training hyperparameters, hardware, inference optimizations, data instructions and access information are unchanged. Appendix J.2.2 corrects only a display heading; its prompt instructions already identify the Advancer in both versions.

R1.justification: The cited works, related-work discussion and substantive positioning against earlier drama-generation and role-playing research are unchanged.

P1.justification: v5 lightly rewrites the abstract, adds Chios Chen and an Independent Researcher affiliation, identifies Shufan Jiang as Project Lead and expands Appendix K’s contributor attribution. It also corrects 'Prompt for Planner' to 'Prompt for Advancer' in J.2.2; section organization is retained.

P2.justification: The expanded author block wraps onto two lines and reflows the first-page abstract and footnotes. Added contributor text shifts the final-page content, and one prompt-box title changes. Figures 1–8 and Tables 1–13 remain visually identical.

improvement.justification: v5 removes a small prompt-heading inconsistency and expands author attribution, while making limited abstract edits. The prompt’s role was already clear from its subsection and instructions in v4. These localized editorial changes leave the scientific argument, evidence and reproducibility information intact, producing no meaningful overall quality difference.
